To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have isolated and characterized two new human ABC transporter genes, ABCC11 (MIM 606819) and ABCC12 (MIM 607079), and mapped them to chromosome 16q.
we cloned and mapped two new human ABCC sub-family genes, ABCC11 (MDR3) and ABCC12 (MVP).

we have identified two new members of human ABC transporters, ABCC11 (MDR3) and ABCC12 (MDR4), which have been mapped to the human genome and are related to the human inherited disease, paroxysmal choreoathetoid disorder.
In summary, our research is concerned with
cloning and characterization of new members of the ABC transporters, with the aim of understanding the role of this superfamily of proteins in human health and disease.
cloning new members of the ABCC gene family, characterizing the genes and their protein products, and determining the role of these genes in human diseases.
the identification and characterization of new genes and the elucidation of their functions, and with the identification of genetic variations in the genes and their association with human disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ABCC gene subfamily has been completed, and the two new members, ABCC11, and ABCC12 have been fully characterized.
ABCC11 is the gene for paroxysomal kinesigenic dyskinesia, while ABCC12 has not been linked to any human disease.
the human ABC transporter superfamily now consists of 49 members, and the human ABCC transporter subfamily consists of 12 members.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the human genome harbors at least 49 ABC transporters, 13 from the ABCA subfamily, 12 from the ABCC subfamily and 24 from the ABCB subfamily.
the human ABC transporter superfamily has 48 identified genes, 29 from the ABCB, ABCD, ABCC and ABCG subfamilies.

we have cloned two new members of ABCC subfamily and mapped them to chromosome 16q, and we are now working on their functional characterization and their potential involvement in human inherited diseases.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the human ABCC gene subfamily has 11 members and that ABCC11 is an important candidate gene for paroxysms of kinesigenic dyskinesia.
we have identified and characterized two new human ABC transporter genes.
the human ABCC gene family is much larger than originally thought and is likely to be even larger as more genes are identified.
